Skills are not loaded into context automatically; this skill queries the skill library (skill-library CLI) to discover and read the skills relevant to the current task. --- # Skill Library Skills are NOT loaded into context automatically. They live in a managed library and must be loaded on demand, per task. ## Workflow — query whenever a skill might help 1. Whenever you think a skill might be needed — before starting a task, when the work shifts into new territory, or when unsure — summarize the task into a 1–3 sentence description (include key technologies, file types, and the goal), then run: ```sh skill-library query "" ``` This fires very often, and that is fine: a query is cheap; a missed skill is not. 2. If matches are returned: Read each returned `path` (absolute paths to skill markdown files) and absorb the instructions **before** working on the task. 3. If `matches` is empty, proceed on your own judgment. 4. For a rapid follow-up that trivially continues the same task with the same context, reusing the skills already read is acceptable; when in doubt, re-query. ## Managing skills Each subcommand has its own skill with the full contract — read it when doing that operation: - `skill-library-query` — scoring the catalog (thresholds, `--top`, stdin, tuning) - `skill-library-list` — browsing the catalog - `skill-library-get` — inspecting one skill / retrieving its content - `skill-library-add` — importing a skill (directory or file) - `skill-library-update` — renaming, rewriting descriptions, re-importing content - `skill-library-remove` — deleting a skill All commands output JSON on stdout, errors on stderr; exit codes 0/1/2. `skill-library --help` for the overview. ## Fallback Run the command before declaring a failure. If it fails, use its stderr and exit code to explain the specific cause briefly: - Binary missing: check `command -v skill-library` and `PATH`. Installing via `npx skills add` installs the skills only; build and install the binary using the [README](https://github.com/ianwijma/skill-library-skill). - Missing `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` or HTTP 401: query needs a valid key in the agent's environment. Never print the key. - Connection error or timeout: online scoring could not reach TypeSafe. Check network/DNS, proxy settings, and agent sandbox restrictions. This does not establish that the service is down; there is no local daemon to start. If the environment reports restricted networking, retry through its supported network-permission mechanism when allowed. Respect denials and use the local fallback when network access is unavailable. - Other exit-2 errors: report the actual diagnostic (for example, an unreadable store), rather than labeling every runtime failure a service outage. When online scoring fails, run `skill-library list` (with the same `--store`, if used). It needs neither network access nor an API key. Select relevant skills from the returned names and descriptions, then read their `path` files before continuing. If the local catalog also fails or has no relevant skills, continue with available guidance. Never block the user's task on the library, and avoid repeating a known failing query during the same task unless conditions change. --- title: use client description: Learn how to use the use client directive to render a component on the client. --- The `'use client'` directive declares an entry point for the components to be rendered on the **client side** and should be used when creating interactive user interfaces (UI) that require client-side JavaScript capabilities, such as state management, event handling, and access to browser APIs. This is a React feature. > **Good to know:** > > You do not need to add the `'use client'` directive to every file that contains Client Components. You only need to add it to the files whose components you want to render directly within Server Components. The `'use client'` directive defines the [server and client boundary](/docs/app/guides/server-and-client-boundary), and the components exported from such a file serve as entry points to the client. ## Usage To declare an entry point for the Client Components, add the `'use client'` directive **at the top of the file**, before any imports. The directive applies to the entire module and cannot be placed inside a component or function: ```tsx filename="app/components/counter.tsx" highlight={1} switcher 'use client' import { useState } from 'react' export default function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0) return (

Count: {count}

) } ``` ```jsx filename="app/components/counter.js" highlight={1} switcher 'use client' import { useState } from 'react' export default function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0) return (

Count: {count}

) } ``` When using the `'use client'` directive, the props of the Client Components must be [serializable](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client#serializable-types). This means the props need to be in a format that React can serialize when sending data from the server to the client. ```tsx filename="app/components/counter.tsx" highlight={4} switcher 'use client' export default function Counter({ onClick /* ❌ Function is not serializable */, }) { return (
) } ``` ```jsx filename="app/components/counter.js" highlight={4} switcher 'use client' export default function Counter({ onClick /* ❌ Function is not serializable */, }) { return (
) } ``` ## Nesting Client Components within Server Components Combining Server and Client Components allows you to build applications that are both performant and interactive: 1. **Server Components**: Use for static content, data fetching, and SEO-friendly elements. 2. **Client Components**: Use for interactive elements that require state, effects, or browser APIs. 3. **Component composition**: Nest Client Components within Server Components as needed for a clear separation of server and client logic. In the following example: - `Header` is a Server Component handling static content. - `Counter` is a Client Component enabling interactivity within the page. ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" highlight={2,8} switcher import Header from './header' import Counter from './counter' // This is a Client Component export default function Page() { return (
) } ``` ```jsx filename="app/page.js" highlight={2,8} switcher import Header from './header' import Counter from './counter' // This is a Client Component export default function Page() { return (
) } ``` ## Reference See the [React documentation](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client) for more information on `'use client'`. # Goal: faithfully recreate Bubble Tanks 3 Continue building a faithful, one-to-one recreation of the original Bubble Tanks 3 Flash game in `/home/ian/Projects/ianwijma/open-bubble-tank`. The intended result is an offline game whose appearance, animation, controls, sound and gameplay are indistinguishable from the original, except for explicitly documented removals and usability additions. The reverse-engineering documentation and original implementation evidence are in `/home/ian/Projects/ianwijma/documented-bubble-tank-3`. Initial research, asset extraction and a demonstration of loading assets directly from the Flash file already exist. Consult that repository whenever functionality is uncertain. Prefer decompiled code, and inspect exported bytecode when the decompiler is ambiguous, rather than inventing behavior. Use Bun, TypeScript, Next.js, Tailwind CSS and the project's selected JavaScript game engine, PixiJS. Keep the implementation lightweight and modular so it can be tinkered with and extended without reworking whole systems. Preserve the separation between simulation, rendering and browser services. Avoid spending time on disposable prototypes when the original provides the specification. Before entering the game, let the player supply their own Flash file. Extract the required artwork and audio locally in the browser using the existing asset-loading approach. Do not bundle or commit the SWF or extracted original media. If no Flash file is supplied, support playable mock assets. Their layouts, sizes, colors and movement should follow the recovered original designs as closely as practical. Strip out currently broken or unavailable functionality, including retired online services, while retaining isolated stubs so those features can be added or restored later. Keep deliberate differences explicit; do not silently reinterpret the original. Continue from the existing implementation rather than restarting. Read `AGENTS.md`, [the continuation handoff](docs/handoff.md), [the architecture](docs/architecture.md) and [the fidelity ledger](docs/fidelity.md). The ledger records implemented contracts, evidence limits and remaining work. The recreation goal is not yet complete: passing selected tests does not establish full-game parity. Verify changes with the appropriate rule tests, browser flows and original-runtime comparisons. Keep documentation current, and occasionally commit and push verified changes using the configured signing setup.
